questions.q: In this CL.TE lab, which length header does each server trust?
o: Front-end uses Transfer-Encoding, back-end uses Content-Length
Front-end uses Content-Length, back-end uses Transfer-Encoding
Both servers use Content-Length and ignore chunked encoding
Both servers use Transfer-Encoding and ignore Content-Length
questions.x: CL.TE means the front-end measures the body with Content-Length. The back-end ends the body with Transfer-Encoding chunked. The lab front-end does not support chunked encoding, which is why that split exists.
questions.h: The name CL.TE lists front-end first, then back-end. CL is Content-Length. TE is Transfer-Encoding.

questions.q: Why were Python raw sockets used instead of curl or the requests library?
o: Those clients lack TLS support for PortSwigger lab hostnames
Those clients cannot send POST bodies larger than thirty bytes
Those clients rewrite length headers, which removes the conflict
Those clients force HTTP/2, and HTTP/2 cannot reach this lab
questions.x: curl and requests try to send valid HTTP. If Transfer-Encoding is chunked, they drop or rewrite Content-Length. The attack needs both headers on the wire, so ssl plus a raw socket sends the bytes unchanged.
questions.h: Well behaved HTTP clients clean conflicting length headers. What does that cleanup destroy?

questions.q: What does a chunk size of 0 mean to the back-end?
o: The rest of the TCP stream should be gzip compressed
The chunked body is finished, later bytes stay buffered
The front-end must close keep-alive before the next send
The request method is silently rewritten from POST to GET
questions.x: Chunked bodies end at a zero-size chunk plus a blank line. The back-end then answers the POST and leaves GET /404 plus X-Ignore unread in its receive buffer.
questions.h: Each chunk starts with a hex size. What does size zero say about whether more body bytes belong to this request?

questions.q: How does a differential 404 confirm the smuggle worked?
o: A later request for / returns 404 because leftover GET /404 ran
The smuggle POST itself returns 404 from the front-end proxy
The back-end returns 404 only when Transfer-Encoding is omitted
Both servers return 404 if the Host header does not match the lab
questions.x: The smuggle POST can still return 200. The leftover prefix turns the next request on that back-end socket into GET /404, so a normal follow-up to / gets 404 Not Found. That flip is the lab solution.
questions.h: The first send can look fine. What unexpected status on a later request to / proves leftover bytes were prepended?

questions.q: What does the X-Ignore: X header in the smuggled prefix do?
o: It tells the front-end to drop leftover GET /404 bytes
It turns off access logging so the 404 is never stored
It absorbs the next request line as a dummy header value
It forces the back-end to answer the smuggle with HTTP/2
questions.x: When the next real request is glued on, its request line becomes the value of X-Ignore. The back-end treats that as an unknown header and still runs the smuggled GET /404.
questions.h: The leftover request is incomplete. Where do the first bytes of the victim request land when the two streams are concatenated?

questions.q: Why does the intended solution require HTTP/1.1?
o: HTTP/2 uses one framing model, so this CL.TE split needs HTTP/1.1
The lab TLS certificate is issued only for HTTP/1.1 user agents
Chunked encoding is disabled unless the client speaks HTTP/1.1
PortSwigger rejects HTTP/2 until a 404 has already been confirmed
questions.x: HTTP/2 has a single framing length. Classic CL.TE smuggling needs HTTP/1.1 ambiguity between Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding. The lab may speak HTTP/2, but this attack is an HTTP/1.1 technique.
questions.h: HTTP/2 does not have two competing body-length headers. Which protocol still does?

questions.q: After the smuggle POST, which unread bytes sit in the back-end buffer?
o: POST / HTTP/1.1 plus the original Content-Length value
The zero-size chunk the front-end refused to forward
The curl User-Agent string from the follow-up GET to /
GET /404 HTTP/1.1 followed by the X-Ignore header prefix
questions.x: The front-end forwards 35 body bytes. The back-end stops at chunk 0, so GET /404 HTTP/1.1 and X-Ignore: X remain unread and become the prefix of the next request on that connection.
questions.h: Look at the bytes after the zero chunk. Which request line is waiting for the next user?

questions.q: In the two-step solve, why can the curl trigger use a new client connection?
o: curl cannot resume a TLS session that a Python socket opened
CORS rules require Python and curl to use different Origin values
Leftover bytes wait on a back-end socket the front-end may reuse
The lab resets every TCP connection after a single request byte
questions.x: The leftover lives on the back-end keep-alive socket, not on the attacker client socket. A new curl to / still works if the front-end reuses that same back-end connection.
questions.h: Python and curl are different clients. Which hop can still reuse a socket that holds the leftover prefix?

questions.q: Which of these statements about this CL.TE lab is correct?
o: The front-end trusts Content-Length
The back-end trusts Content-Length
X-Ignore drops leftover GET /404 bytes
All of these statements are true
questions.x: The front-end trusts Content-Length, which is the CL in CL.TE. The back-end trusts Transfer-Encoding, not Content-Length. X-Ignore absorbs the next request line as a dummy header value, it does not drop GET /404. All is wrong because those last two claims are false.
questions.h: CL.TE names the front-end header first. Which length header does this front-end actually use?

questions.q: Which of these statements about this lab is correct?
o: curl leaves both length headers untouched
The front-end parses the body as chunked
Solving the lab requires smuggling /admin
None of these statements are true
questions.x: curl rewrites conflicting length headers. The front-end uses Content-Length, not chunked encoding. The lab is solved when a later request to / gets 404, not by reaching /admin.
questions.h: Would a well behaved HTTP client keep both length headers? Does this front-end speak chunked? Is /admin the goal?
